exam: A 28‑year‑old man presents with a progressive thoracic hump and low back pain. What is the first investigation you would order? — X‑ray standing AP/lateral to measure Cobb angle and look for vertebral collapse.
A patient with kyphosis has a normal Mantoux but a high ESR. What is the next step? — Consider spinal TB; start empirical ATT while awaiting imaging.
You observe a patient with a thoracic hump but no neurological signs. What conservative treatment is appropriate? — Bracing with thoracolumbosacral orthosis and physiotherapy.
A child with kyphosis shows a rapid increase in hump size over 2 weeks. What red flag does this raise? — Possible spinal cord compression; urgent MRI and referral.
Which drug should be avoided in a patient with kyphosis and known liver disease? — NSAIDs, due to hepatotoxicity risk.
During ward rounds you notice a patient with kyphosis and a normal chest X‑ray. What could still explain the deformity? — Early vertebral collapse not yet visible, or congenital vertebral anomaly.
ai.title: Kyphosis
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Kyphosis is an exaggerated posterior thoracic curvature that can arise from structural, infectious or developmental causes. Clinical assessment focuses on spinal alignment, neuro‑signs and underlying etiology, especially spinal TB in low‑resource settings.

b: Loss of normal thoracic kyphosis curve
sections.p: Kyphosis is a forward curvature of the thoracic spine exceeding 45° on a Cobb measurement or a visible hump on the back. Diagnosis combines history, inspection, palpation and, where available, imaging.

t.b: Assess thoracic curvature angle – >45° confirms kyphosis
Measures Cobb angle, identifies vertebral collapse or deformity; also detects TB lesions
Evaluates spinal cord compression, abscesses; used when TB suspected and resources allow

sections.p: Severity is graded by Cobb angle and functional impact. In TB, the GATA staging (I–IV) guides treatment urgency.

t.b: Quantifies curvature; >45° warrants surgical consideration in adults
I: minimal collapse; II: moderate; III: severe collapse with kyphosis >30°; IV: severe collapse with neurological deficit

b: Spinal TB – vertebral body destruction and collapse
sections.p: In East Africa, spinal tuberculosis (Pott’s disease) is the leading cause of kyphosis. Other common etiologies include congenital vertebral anomalies, severe osteoporosis, and post‑traumatic deformity.

t.b: Screen for TB exposure; positive supports TB suspicion
Shows paravertebral abscess, vertebral collapse, or calcified lesions
Elevated in active infection; helps monitor response

b: Weakness, numbness or tingling in lower limbs if cord involved
sections.p: Patients may report back pain, progressive hump, restricted chest expansion, or neurological deficits if cord compression occurs.
Prioritize affordable tests; if imaging unavailable, clinical signs guide urgency.

t.b: Detects vertebral collapse, kyphosis angle, TB lesions; if unavailable, proceed to clinical assessment and empirical TB treatment if high suspicion
Supports TB diagnosis; positive suggests need for anti‑TB therapy
High values indicate active inflammation; used to monitor treatment response

b: Respiratory compromise – severe kyphosis can restrict lung function
sections.p: Neurological deficit, severe pain, rapid progression, or systemic signs of infection warrant urgent referral.

b: Bracing – thoracolumbosacral orthosis if Cobb >45° and no neurological deficit
sections.p: Treat underlying cause first; in TB, anti‑tubercular therapy (ATT) is essential. Supportive care includes pain control, physiotherapy and bracing.

b: Ensure adequate calcium and vitamin D intake
sections.p: Regular clinical review, repeat imaging at 3–6 months, and monitoring for drug toxicity. Prevention focuses on TB control, early fracture management and nutritional support.

b: Pectus excavatum – chest depression, not spinal curvature
sections.p: Scoliosis (lateral curvature), pectus excavatum/carinatum (chest wall deformity), and post‑traumatic kyphosis.

b: ESR normal in chronic low‑grade infection
sections.p: Low‑grade TB may show normal Mantoux; early vertebral collapse can appear normal on X‑ray; ESR can be normal in chronic disease.

whenToSeekHelp: Neurological deficit (weakness, numbness), severe back pain, rapid hump progression, fever or weight loss indicating active TB, respiratory compromise
